Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are two inflammatory diseases affecting the muscles. While they share some similarities, they do not affect the same muscle groups.

Dermatomyositis primarily affects the muscles of the upper and lower limbs, particularly those in the proximal region, such as the biceps, brachialis, triceps, and coracobrachialis. These affected muscles are located in areas close to the posterior compartments of the thigh.

Polymyositis, on the other hand, primarily affects the skeletal muscles throughout the body, including the thigh muscles. However, it tends to affect more proximal muscles, such as those in the anterior compartment of the thigh.

Although both diseases can cause similar symptoms, such as muscle weakness and fatigue, they do not typically affect the same muscle groups or patterns. In fact, PM is often associated with a more pronounced involvement of the posterior compartments of the thigh, whereas DM tends to have more bilateral (both sides) involvement.

To target physiotherapy effectively at the most frequently affected muscles in each condition, it's essential to consider individual cases and muscle group specificities. For example, if you have PM, you may need to focus on strengthening the posterior thigh muscles, including those in the gluteus medius and piriformis muscles, which are often involved. In contrast, DM primarily affects the biceps, brachialis, and triceps muscles in the proximal upper limb.

In summary, while dermatomyositis and polymyositis share some similarities, they do not affect similar thigh muscles. Each condition requires a tailored approach to physiotherapy based on individual muscle group specificities and symptoms.
